RECONSTRUCTED TEXT — Open Library search-inside, 2026-09-06
===========================================================
THE McGILL YOU KNEW: AN ANTHOLOGY OF MEMORIES, 1920-1960
(Don Mills, Ont.: Longman Canada, 1975). Internet Archive: isbn_0774700130 — scan leaf 314.

NOT A SCAN. The book is lending-restricted and has not been read. The passage was assembled from
overlapping twelve-word windows returned by https://openlibrary.org/search/inside.json (contract at
f_4933), walked to a chapter break. Page images return HTTP 403.

FOUND BY THE NAME SWEEP. The query was `"Hay Finlay"` — one of the names in this project's own
`directors-index.md` that had never been run against the book corpus.


RECOVERED PASSAGE (continuous; two runs from the same leaf)
-----------------------------------------------------------

    "... Shag Shaughnessy, Bert Light, Van Wagner, George Vickerson, Frank Saxton, HAY FINLAY and
    our chief sport administrator, Major Stuart ...

    ... — which was usually in doubt till near the end. In the off season, Van and Hay Finlay, the
    gymnastics and soccer coach, developed Camp Nominingue in County Labelle, where many students
    worked as counsellors in the summer. Though a private venture, the camp was closely connected
    with the university by personal associations, and was known as 'Camp McGill' to all the
    residents of the area. CHAPTER ..."

("Camp McGeell" is the OCR; the word is McGill.)


WHY IT MATTERS, AND THE PART THAT IS THIS PROJECT'S OWN FAULT
-------------------------------------------------------------

Hay Finlay is in `wiki/people/directors-index.md` as Kamp Kanawana's SENIOR SECTION DIRECTOR IN
1922, "ex-Central YMCA Boys' Physical Director, then at McGill Physical Education", from the camp's
own 1922 brochure (f_0056).

He is also, in this project's KNOWLEDGE BASE, the co-founder of Camp Nominingue:

  f_2641 — Anne Vail's 1954 profile of F. M. Van Wagner: "He was co-founder of this Camp with HAY
           FINLAY in 1925."
  f_3039 — G. H. Merrill's February 1963 profile: "In the fall of 1924, Van and a McGill associate
           of his, Hay Finlay, decided that they would operate their own camp."
  f_2476 — the Canadian Camping Association executive of February 1949: "Secretary-Treasurer Hay
           Finlay, 475 Pine Ave West, Montreal."

Both f_2641 and f_3039 say IN THEIR OWN TEXT that the KB already holds him as Kanawana's 1922
section director. And `canadian-camping-movement.md`'s Open Question 4 went on saying, through
several revisions and as recently as this week, that **"no named individual confirmed on both sides
of the connection so far"**, recording that Camp Nominingue's counsellor Marc Beique had been
checked specifically and produced nothing.

**The question was not unanswered. It was unread.** The article and the knowledge base were never
run against each other on this point. That is the fifteenth rule in the 2026-09-06 handoff — *use
the knowledge base as a test of the articles, not only as a source for them* — and this is its
second demonstration in two days, after the seventh split in the plaque index.


WHAT THIS BOOK ADDS ON TOP OF THE JOIN
--------------------------------------
- Finlay's actual job: **gymnastics and soccer coach** at McGill, named among the university's
  coaching staff of the period.
- Nominingue's character: a private camp **staffed by McGill students**, "closely connected with the
  university by personal associations", and known locally as **"Camp McGill"**.
- Which sharpens the Kanawana question rather than closing it: the channel between Kanawana and the
  Laurentian private-camp world in the 1920s was PERSONAL — coaches and students moving between a
  university department, a YMCA camp and a private camp — and not institutional.

NOT ESTABLISHED: Finlay's first name (every source gives "Hay Finlay"), his dates, how long he
stayed at Nominingue, or whether he had any further connection with Kanawana after 1922. Note also
that this project holds a competing account of Camp Nominingue's origins from a 2016 Quebec history
(f_4939) which gives 1911 and calls it "le premier camp francophone"; the 1924-25 founding by Van
Wagner and Finlay is what the camping association's own magazine says twice, and the two accounts
are not reconciled here.
